OUTRAGED.
An Attempt to Lynch a Villain Frustrated by the Police.
ELYRIA, May 11.—At about 9 o'clock Sunday night last Miss Eva Broughton, a young lady about sixteen years of age, living on Lake avenue, while returning from church alone was overtaken at the avenue crossing of the Tuscarawas Valley and Wheeling Railway Company by a dastardly villain, who stepped up behind her, tbrew her down, and by choking her and threatening her with a revolver, kept her quiet while he outraged her. As soon as she could escape she fled for her home and, although nearly crazed, told her story and described the appearance of the man. She has since been in a critical condition from the injury and nervous shock. Yesterday a young man by the name of George Wells, an employee of the Elyria Screw and Tap Company, was arrested on suspicion. He was escorted to the girl's house, and she identified him. While he was at the house with the officers, some of Wells' fellow workmen and some neighbors heard that the girl had identified him as the man who had committed the outrage, and they gathered about the house with the purpose of lynching him on the spot, but the officers managed to elude them, and Wells was brought before Squire Doolittle, when he waived an examination, and in default of bail was sent to jail. If he is the man, as now seems extremely probable, it will go hard with him. There will be no lynching, but he will receive no mercy from the court or jury when his trial comes.

DESPERATE RAILROADERS.
Great Excitement Among Laborers at the Reduction of Their Wages-If General-Manager Moxie
Had Been at Wildhorse Last Monday the Texas Pacific Would Have Been an Official Short.
Sr. Louis, January 13.—The story comes up from Texas that the section hands and other laborers on the Texas Pacific railroad are greatly excited over the recent reduction of their wages to $1 15 per day, and that, four days ago, a large party of them stopped the pay-car at a point called Wildhorse, under the impression that it was General-Manager Hoxie's car and that he was aboard of it. They side-tracked it and demanded the delivery of Mr. Hoxie that they might lynch him. When told that that official was not in the car the mob would not believe it, and they piled up wood around the car to fire it, and, as they said, roast Hoxie out. Paymaster Kretz finally made the excited men comprehend that Mr. Hoxie was not present, but they kept the car on the side track two days before they allowed it to go East. It is also said that great dissatisfaction exists at other points along the line, and that a considerable number of mechanics have been discharged from the shops at Marshall. It is also stated that there is to be a general reduction of wages soon. If this is carried out the men say there will be trouble.

A Mob After a Pay-car.
The colored porter, late in the employe of Paymaster Kretz, of the Texas & Pacific Railway, broke a bit of news here Thursday night which was at first not credited, though on investigation it was found that he told the truth. The facts have been kept quiet for the past ten days. At that time Paymaster Kretz went west over the line to settle with the employes of the road. On reaching a station a short distance this side of El Paso the car was halted by an armed lot of laborers who demanded their pay. These men, it appears, had belonged to the grading force and for some reason Mr. Kretz did not have them down on his pay list. The men were considerably excited and threatened destruction to the car, which they detained four or five hours, by which time Paymaster Kretz had convinced them of their error, when the train was permitted to pass on.

Chicago, Ill., April 17.—Contradictory reports have been received as to the lynching of the murderer of Mr. Stubbs, of Polk City, Iowa, but all reliable statements ase to the effect that the report is untrue, although in the existing state of excitement such an event is likely to occur in case the murderer can be identified.
job-weise-polk-city-1882-04-01.A4:
Murderers Saved from Lynching.
Des Moines, Iowa. April 17.—The funer
Murderers Saved from Lynching.
DES MOINES, Iowa, April 17.—The funeral of R. W. Stubbs, the murdered Mayor of Polk city, was held yesterday, the Odd Fellows and the Ancient Order of United Workmen conducting the ceremonies. The procession to the cemetery was over a mile in length. A large delegation attended from this city. Five arrests have been made, and one suspected man is still at large. The prisoners were guarded by vigilants until train time this evening, when they were turned over to the officers. They were taken on board, but when ready to depart the vigilants rallied, boarded the train, opened a switch, placed an armed man at each brake and refused to let the train start. One prisoner was taken off and efforts made to secure the others. Prominent citizens appealed to the leaders, pleading that the law should be allowed to take its course, and they were finally persuaded to permit the prisoners to be brought to this city, where they are now safely lodged in the county jail. It is thought the excitement will die out and that the danger of lynching is passed.

Murdered at Midnight
Bines Special to Chicago Tim
Des Moines Special to Chicago Times: R. M. Stubbs, mayor of the town of Polk City, a station on the Chicago & Northwestern railway, was murdered in his house at 3 o'clock this (Saturday) morning by two unknown assassins, who entered his house by the rear window, passing through the kitchen, dining, and sitting rooms to the hall and stairway. Mrs. Stubbs and her husband occupied a room at the head of the stairs, and while making the ascent the wife heard them and aroused her husband. Mr. Stubbs arose in bed and asked what was wanted. The answer came back, emphasized with profane and obscene words: "Lie down, or you will be shot." Mr. Stubbs told the intruder to get out, and sprang out of bed. As he did so a dark lantern was turned on him and a pistol shot was fired, the ball striking him in the left breast, just below the nipple, penetrating his heart. He staggered to the head of the stairs, toothed a moment, and fell headlong down the flight, a corpse. The murderers immediately fled through the front door, mounted horses, which had been posted near the front gate, and rapidly disappeared in the night. The object of the murderers was evidently burglary. The murdered man was a member of the milling firm of Eggleston & Stubbs. Some time last summer their safe was blown open and robbed of its contents. Since that time the funds of the firm have been kept by Mr. Stubbs in his house, as there is no bank in Polk City. He was also treasurer of the school district and of the Odd Fellows lodge. In these several capacities he would naturally handle a considerable amount of funds. His bankers in Des Moines state that he had not deposited anything with them recently, and they are of the opinion that he had quite a sum of money in his possession, some estimating it as high as $7,000. The assassins were no doubt after the money when their presence was discovered. None of it was secured, however. The murder created the most intense excitement in Polk county. Mr. Stubbs was a man of noble qualities, and universally esteemed. The terrible manner of his taking off has fallen with a great shock on the community. Suspicion rests upon two men, one from Des Moines, and the other from the vicinity of Polk City. The town has a well organized company of vigilantees, who have done duty in emergencies before. They are out in force, and should they capture the murderers of the man, the State will be spared the trouble of inflicting the penalty. Sheriff Littleton has remained to

DES MOINES, Io., June 27.—A young man named Delaire, arrested in the depot of Polk City last night on suspicion of being the murderer of R. P. Stubbs, mayor of that city, last April, under threat of lynching confessed that a gang of fifteen had plotted to rob Stubbs and brought two desperadoes, Wicks and Blackman, to do the work, and that Wicks did the killing. Quite an affecting incident took place at the state prison at Stillwater Saturday. A bright little Norwegian boy about eight years old called at the office of the Northwestern Manufacturing and Car company inquiring for his father, who said he had written his mother that he had a steady situation for that firm and the little fellow had come from his home in a distant locality to pay him a visit. His face was wreathed in smiles and beamed with happy expectation. What was his surprise when informed that his father was a convict and was sentenced to a life long imprisonment for the crime of murder. How sudden the transformation. The face but a moment before so cheerful and hapoy was now clouded and hot tears fast coursed down them. The little fellow left the office weeping bitterly.

End of a Notorious Outlaw.
Tremendous excitement was caused at St. Joseph, Mo., on the 3d inst., by the announcement that Jesse James, the notorious bandit and robber had been killed at his temporary residence in that city. The news spread with great rapidity and crowds of people soon assembled at the little frame shanty in the southwestern part of the city where lay the dead body of the notorious freebooter whose name had grown to be a terror in the southwest. The shooting, which was done by Charles and Robert Ford, who had long been intimates of James, was accomplished in a cowardly manner, and although the country is well rid of a dangerous character by their act, fair-minded people cannot but harbor contempt for the Fords.

Jesse James and wife arrived in St. Joseph in November last, since which time they lived quietly in the little house where the tragedy was enacted. The Ford boys occupied a room in the rear of the house, and while they professed friendship and loyalty to their chief, and even planned with him to rob a bank at Platte City, they had a secret understanding to kill Jesse since last fall and thus secure the $50,000 reward offered by the state of Missouri for the body of the outlaw, either dead or alive. The opportunity presented itself on the morning of the 3d inst. Breakfast had just been eaten and Charles Ford and Jesse James had been in the stable grooming their horses preparatory to their night's ride. On returning to the house James complained of the heat and divested himself of his vest and belt which contained two revolvers and a quantity of cartridges. He then picked up a duster, stepped up on a chair and commenced dusting a picture which hung on the wall, his back being turned to the Fords. Both Robert and Charles immediately drew their weapons, but the former was the quickest and sent a ball crashing through their chief's brain. Mrs. James, who was in the kitchen, immediately rushed to her stricken husband and was loud in her lamentations. Mrs. James acknowledged her husband's identity, saying that she long expected the tragic event which would make her a widow. A ring taken from the dead man's finger, marked "Jesse James" is also taken as convincing evidence that the deceased is none other than the famous bandit. The Ford boys immediately surrendered themselves to the sheriff and made a statement of their action. They said they had been on James' track for a long time. It is believed they were with James in some of his exploits and were influenced to kill James by the heavy rewards offered.

ARRESTED.—About one year ago Bazeleel Yauger, who lived on the headwaters of Thirteen Mile Creek, was arrested on the charge of lunacy, and after an examination before a Justice, was adjudged a lunatic. His wife, Mary Yauger, giving bond for his "conduct and proper care," took charge of him and kept him at her house. Some three weeks since Mr. Yauger disappeared, and suspicion of foul play being aroused, his brothers and friends made diligent search through the woods and about the premises, but their efforts to find him failed. They then went to the house of his wife and asked the privilege of searching the house. This request was denied them, and accompanied with the threat that "if anyone attempted to enter the house there would be blood shed." Such conduct on their part added to the excitement and suspicions of the friends of Yauger, and they began to watch the house at night. During one of these watches at a late hour of the night, they saw a light in the window, and heard a noise as if some one pounding on the floor, which was followed by a noise as if a box was being dragged across the floor. In searching the woods they found notices posted upon the trees, requesting Baz to come home to sign a deed, and signed "Mary Yauger." All this added to the suspicions and probabilities that Yauger had been murdered, and on last Thursday, Henry Yauger, a brother of the missing man, made complaint before Justice Franklin, who issued a warrant for the arrest of Mary Yauger, Miranda Miller, Charles Miller and his wife. The parties were arrested by Deputy Sheriff Geo. Daugherty, and brought before Justice Franklin on Saturday last. The State not being ready, the parties were committed to jail to await an examination fixed for to day.

The body of Jordan Thompson, colored, was found near Graball last Sunday with the head cut off. Jack Lewis, Adam Felder, Andrew Watts and Lizzie, wife of the murdered man were at once arrested and G. W. Brooks, justice of the peace and A. D. Gee, constable were sent for to hold an inquest, and upon their arrival at Graball, Jake Lewis and Adam Felder were turned over to constable Gee and soon afterward Andrew Watts and Lizzie Thompson were delivered to him; he held them at Grabhll till Monday when they were all taken to Washington by deputy sheriff Spencer and posse. The jury of inquest at Graball returned a verdict that deceased was murdered by the three men arrested. A preliminary examination was held at Washington by Justice Brooks. The complaint was read to the prisoners by the justice and all of them plead not guilty except Jake Lewis, who plead guilty notwithstanding the justice cautioned him. Jake said that he killed Thompson and did not want others to suffer for his act. After hearing all the testimony and there being no evidence against the other parties the justice released them, holding Jake Lewis without bail. The prisoner was placed in charge of constable Gee, who on account of high water was compelled to bring his prisoner round by rail arriving here on the Central Tuesday night and turning his prisoner over to the sheriff at the county jail. Constable Gee reports that while he was asleep at his home in Washington, Monday night, three masked men attempted to rescue the prisoner from the guard, but fortunately Mr. Gee was notified in time to prevent it. The guard think that the parties who attempted the rescue were negroes. During the trial the excitement was very high and guards had to be placed at the doors of the courthouse by the constable to keep the crowd back. Jack claims that he killed Thompson because he threatened his life; no proof of this was elicited at the trial. The killing was done with a club and the subsequent decapitation with an axe.

In the First Ward, beyond the quarreling, every thing past off quietly and a large vote was polled. Some of the Democrats then tried to raise a disturbance, although the man had turned to go away. Police officers Ryan and Hardy rushed in the crowd, when they were told by Mr. Vickers that there was no call for their interference. The officers then grabbed hold of Mr. Vickers and although he made no resistance, Hardy took him by the throat and beat him on the head until he was insensible, and would no doubt have killed him had not some bystanders interfered. He was then dragged up to the hall, with these so called guardians of the peace cursing and threatening him all the way. On the way up he asked not to be taken past his residence as his wife was lying very ill.

The officers met this request with curses, and told him that was the way they intended to take him. Although the blood was streaming from the wounds in his head and almost blinding him, they refused to even let him wipe it off. He was not detained at the hall but a few minutes, when he was released and allowed to go to his home, where medical attendance was secured and leeches applied by Mr. Parker. Mr. Vickers was confined to his bed yesterday from his injuries. This certainly is one of the greatest outrages ever committed in this city, and some action should be taken to punish the perpetrators. Mr. Vickers is an honest, industrious citizen, a member of Asbury M. E. church, and has been in the emplow of the P. W. & B. The Imprisoned Miners Rescued.

SAN FRANCISCO, June 4.—A dispatch from Virginia City says: "Six men penetrated the Alta drift to-night with refreshments for the imprisoned miners. All wore ice helmets, to enable them to pass the belt of 800 feet of foul air between the entrance and the end of the drift. The men were found in comparatively good condition. They had turned water from the drift into their ice-water keg when empty, twisted the end of the compressed air pipe into a barrel of water, and, standing around it, breathed the air thus cooled as it arose through the water. About midnight all were removed from the drift, the whistles along the lode signaling the event. The bodies of Bennett and Callahan, the brave fellows who perished in the attempt to rescue the miners by means of a boat, have been recovered."

CHICAGO, June 4.—A dispatch from Fort Apache, Arizona, says: "A courier from Captain Kramer's camp at Forestdale, brings intelligence of Indian depredations, in which one man was killed and some stock driven off. Captain Kramer and citizens went in pursuit of the Indians toward the Cibicu country. Pedro and part of his band of White Mountain Indians were having a war dance when the courier left. It was thought, however, that they did not intend going on the war path. It is believed the depredations were committed by Cibicu Indians and part of Pedro's young men whom he could not control. The courier was fired on and pursued some distance from camp. A troop of the Sixth Cavalry has been dispatched to Kramer's assistance."

Anxious to Fight a Duel.

TROY, June 4.—Captain Twamley and Commander Keith met by chance in the Budget office last night, when Keith said: "I've been looking for you." "Well, I am on hand," replied Twamley, "and I mean just what I said in my challenge. I want you to understand right here and now that I will meet you when and where you say, and give you the choice of weapons. You have lied about me, and I don't propose to stand it." Keith said he would meet Twamley, but did not say when. Twamley being shown a published paragraph this afternoon that his challenge was considered a hoax, asserted that he was in earnest, and that Keith dare not meet him.

A Republican Victory.

WILMINGTON, DEL., June 4.—Complete returns from all the wards in the city show the election of the Republican ticket by majorities of about 150. The Republicans elect a majority of the council. The total vote for the city was: For Mayor, Dr. J. P. Wales, (Rep.) 4,284; Joseph L. Carpente, (Dem.) 4,152; city treasurer, J. Eldridge Pierce, (Rep.) 4,354; John Guthrie, (Dem.) 4,053; president of the council, Henry C. Conrad, (Rep.) 4,320; Robert H. Taylor, (Dem.) 4,119. The Republicans elect seven councilmen, which with five holding over and the president gives them a majority of three. The Democrats elect eight councilmen.
